## Methods

Population inclusion, community engagement and ethics
Irrespective of gender, 190 study participants (genetically determined as 99 female; 91 male) greater than 18 years, with a preference for older community members belonging to a Khoe-San language group (n=150) were recruited within the borders of Namibia (Supplementary Information 1 and https://www.hayeslab.net/videos) as part of the Diversity inclusive Genome Study for Southern Africa (DiGS-SA), a subsidiary of the Southern African Prostate Cancer Study (SAPCS) Namibia, under informed consent following extensive community discussions and continued engagement. Community over individual compensation, including addressing of community-specific needs, was provided post-initial sampling and under the guidance of the community members. Within South Africa, participants were recruited as part of the University of Limpopo Ubuntu Genomics Project (see https://www.hayeslab.net/videos), a subsidiary of the SAPCS and aimed to represent country-specific ethnolinguistic diversity broadly defined as Bantu, SAC and European (n=30). As participants were sourced from volunteered university staff and students, no participant compensation was received. We have previously reported on ancient Khoe-San heritage within South African Bantu and SAC communities while addressing cultural considerations based on population identifier terminologies. In brief, while Khoe-San (or Khoi-San) languages are grouped through their use of click consonants, Bantu includes a large group of non-click languages with Southern African exceptions such as isiXhosa and isiZulu having historically incorporated click consonants. All study participants self-identified back to two generations; final population labels indicated where the person lived, and mostly self-identified, although recognising the mixed heritage.

The research presented was performed in accordance with the ethical standards of the overseeing human research ethics committees (HREC) and local governance, as per the 1964 Helsinki Declaration. In Namibia, the study was reviewed and approved by the Ministry of Health and Social Services (MoHSS 17/3/3 HEAF003 2024 latest update; previously 17/3/3 HAYES 2008 and 17/3/3 HEYNS 2014) and in South Africa by the University of Pretoria HREC (43/2010 2022 latest update, merged with 280/2017 and including US Federal wide assurance FWA00002567 and IRB00002235 IORG0001762) and the University of Limpopo Faculties of Health Sciences (MREC/HS/214/2011). Samples were shipped to Australia in accordance with institutional and governmental Material Transfer Agreements (MTAs) and including the Republic of South Africa Department of Health Export Permit (National Health Act 2003, J1/2/4/2 No 1/12). WGS and analysis was performed in accordance with the approval granted by St. Vincent’s Hospital Human Research Ethics Committee (SVH/15/227).

WGS, data processing and variant calling
DNA extracted from blood underwent 2×150 bp sequencing on the Illumina HiSeq X instrument (Kinghorn Centre for Clinical Genomics, Garvan Institute of Medical Research). Raw sequencing reads were aligned against human reference hg38+alternative contigs using bwa (v.0.7.15). The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK, v.3.5-0) was used for duplicate marking, indel realignment and base quality recalibration. Germline small variants were identified using two callers (HaplotypeCaller and FreeBayes). We also processed whole-genome raw reads of 22 African genomes and two Asian genomes reported in a previous publication using our unified pipeline. Full details of the unified analysis are provided in Supplementary Information 2. The discovery of genomic rearrangements (short tandem repeats and mobile element insertions) using WGS data is detailed in Supplementary Information 5.

Familial relatives and quality control
We searched for close family relatives by computing, for each pair of individuals, sample mix-ups (using 1,484,044 SNVs and discordance cut-off at 0.20; Supplementary Data 2), kinship coefficients and identical by descent segments (using 15,603,438 SNVs) and exclusion of 1st-degree relationships (full-sib and parent-offspring). Joint-genotyping variation data suitable for downstream analyses were assessed through different analysis pipelines and genotyping/sequencing technologies for their concordance (Supplementary Data 3). The detailed explanation is provided in Supplementary Information 3 and Supplementary Fig. 1c, d.

Merged data of published present-day human and ancient genomes
We retrieved 380 relevant individuals from 13 present-day African populations genotyped on the Human Origins array and the Illumina Omni bead chip, and included published ancient South African genomes and high-coverage genomes from the Human Diversity Genome Project (HGDP) and 1000 Genomes Project (1000GP), including 2,778 individuals from 67 worldwide populations defined by gnomAD v3.1. After merging with our whole genomes and filtering with a minor allele frequency >0.01 and a missing genotyping rate <0.1, we obtained 93,976 autosomal SNVs across the worldwide populations. Kinship analysis (KING; Supplementary Information 3) was performed to remove 1st-degree relations, with a threshold of 0.177. More details are provided in Supplementary Data 7.

Population structure
In total, 143 Khoe-San and 33 regionally relevant genomes (this study), 28 previously published African genomes (SAPCS and SGDP) and 179 reference individuals from the 1000GP (Africans, African Americans and Eurasians) contained 7,003,530 filtered variants computed for robust population structure analyses (Supplementary Information 6). For ADMIXTURE v1.3.0 analyses of K=2–15 (10 replicates each) using the default five-fold cross validation, the above-mentioned merged dataset of high-coverage genomes was filtered for a minor allele frequency >0.1, individual missing genotype data <0.1 and variant call rate >0.9 and then pruned for linkage disequilibrium in PLINK v2.0 using a window size of 50 bp, a step size of 10 bp, and a r^2 threshold of 0.1, leaving 289,025 SNVs among 2964 individuals. Pong v1.5 was used to check for concordance between replicates for each K and for visualisation.

The non-linear dimension reduction UMAP method provided fine-scale relationships between geography and ethnolinguistic identities in Khoe-San populations, analysing our merged dataset with or without samples with genotyping arrays. Principal component analyses of six groups deeply sequenced (San, Damara, SAC, South African European, Herero-Himba and West African Niger-Congo; Supplementary Data 1) were computed across different variant types (SNV, indel, STR and MEI) as described in Supplementary Information 4, 5.

Phylogenomic analysis
The large-scale Maximum Likelihood tree of 16,083 genes from 33 ancestrally distinguishable genomes identified in this study and the Altai Neanderthal published previously was reconstructed using RAxML, as revealed in Supplementary Information 7. In total, whole-genome diploid consensus sequences encompassing 137,927 exons or 26,039,475 bp were converted from analysis-ready GATK data. Local alignment of those sequences was performed, and an extended majority-rule consensus phylogeny was built by reconciling the best tree with 100,000 bootstrap searches, using Altai Neanderthal as an outgroup. Eight individuals with insufficient phylogenetic signals were removed in a final phylogeny using the RogueNaRok programme.

Patterns of derived variation and doubleton allele sharing
Joint-called consensus SNV data using the two callers described above were used to infer derived variation, with ancestral state inferred from ancestral hg38 genome (Ensembl compara 93 database). Coding and noncoding regions were functionally annotated, with further details provided in Supplementary Information 4. Rare doubleton variants observed twice across the autosomal DNA dataset were identified across the 143 Khoe-San genomes using the biallelic SNV data. Loci that had missing genotypes greater than 10% were removed. We calculated f4 and D-statistics of those derived variants at different frequency intervals (≤0.1, 0.1–0.2, 0.2–0.3, 0.3–0.4, 0.4–0.5, 0.5–0.6, 0.6–0.7, 0.8–0.9 and >0.9) using the ADMIXTOOLS2 programme and reported D values and |Z|>3 as significant. We compared f-statistics between forager populations and Niger-Congo/Herero-Himba speakers to address a relationship between forager populations and admixture from neighbouring populations.

Admixture proportion and dating
We reconstructed the timeframe of admixture waves between major ancestral components in Khoe-San populations using the fast GLOBETROTTER programme. We followed the programme instruction for the analysis of 69 San, 63 Damara and 11 Nama genomes in this study, together with the merged WGS data described above and phased by SHAPEIT2. In brief, ChromoPainter v2 was run to estimate the effective population size and mutation rate of the data (407.590 and 0.000441, respectively). It painted haplotypically phased chromosomes of targeted admixed individuals with the haplotypes of all other individuals from other reference populations (113 Italy, 108 LWK, 18 Southern Bantu and 127 YRI genomes).

Population size and separation
We used the Pairwise Sequentially Markovian Coalescent (PSMC) to infer population sizes using a single diploid genome per population that was scaled with a generation time of 30 years and a mutation rate of 1.25×10^−8 mutations per nucleotide per generation. We used MSMC2 to estimate changes in population split times. This analysis used phased genome datasets and eight haplotypes (two genomes from each of a pair of populations). By expected site-frequency spectrum models using momi2, we also simulated all possible pairwise population divergence times under simple, clean split scenarios (20–500 kya). Diploid effective size and recombination rate parameters were set to 12,000 and 1.25×10^−8, respectively. More information is shown in Supplementary Information 8.

To complement the above-mentioned coalescent-based methods, Relate v1.2.2 was employed using 21 Damara and 30 Yoruba, with no suggestive admixture signals defined in this study to avoid deep coalescence time of San contribution in this tree-based analysis as shown in Supplementary Fig. 6b. Biallelic SNV consensus data (2 callers) were phased using SHAPEIT2 and filtered by the 1000GP accessible genome pilot mask to keep only passed positions. Ancestral/derived alleles for each SNV were defined by the human ancestor GRCh37 e59 before within-population and cross-population coalescence rates were computed using the EstimatePopulationSize.sh script. Using IBDNe, the ancestry-specific effective population size was estimated. We followed the guidelines provided by the authors, using our merged dataset of WGS and genotype data. Local ancestry information was inferred using 20 San, 20 Damara, 38 Southern Bantu and 113 Italian genomes from this study and previous publications as reference source populations.

Genome assembly-based analysis of positive selection
To assess the impact of positive selection on shaping human diversity and its relevance to population fitness, we have developed amino acid-based selection tests using de novo genome assemblies (see the Code availability section). The main steps of this analysis include i) generating an individual’s genome draft; ii) extracting sample-specific target sequences; iii) generating cohort-wise multiple sequence alignment per gene; iv) performing local and amino acid-guided alignment methods; and v) positive selection tests. Full details of analysis steps, parameters and relevant tests are provided in Supplementary Information 9, 10.

Alternative methods to identifying potential SNVs under positive selection in forager populations (admixture fraction <30%; 55 San and 56 Damara individuals) were computed using PBS and XP-EHH statistics. PBS utilises pairwise Fst values of exonic regions among three populations to quantify genetic differentiation along each branch of their corresponding three-population tree using 60 CEU genomes from 1000GP as a control to find outlier PBS scores. Normalised XP-EHH of phasing variant data detected selected variants that were near fixation in one forager group but not in the CEU population using the rehh package in R. Only SNVs with minor allele frequency >0.01 were considered while phased with a reference panel of haplotypes following SHAPEIT2 guidelines for the XP-EHH analysis. To identify candidate regions for selection, we then averaged the XP-EHH over windows of length 100,000 bp with a step length of one kb between windows; the windows chosen were required to have >50 SNVs and represented the top 1% with the highest percentage of outlier scores.

Khoe-San signatures for local adaptation
Medical Genome Reference Bank (MGRB) is a catalogue of deep whole-genome variation across thousands of healthy elderly individuals, mostly of European descent, with no reported history of cancer, cardiovascular disease, or dementia. Comparing this resource acts as a control population when linking to Khoe-San genomes and assists in variant filtering and assignment of pathogenicity for genetic traits (Supplementary Information 10). To identify outliers between the forager genomes (San and Damara, n=111) and the control population, Manhattan plots of positively selected variants were visualised with -log P>4.301, with the analysis of their potential in functional biology via ANNOVAR and significance in trait association through multiple databases (i.e., PharmGKB, GPCRdb, GWAS Catalogue, and GTEx). We generated homology protein models of G protein-coupled receptors, and the modelled protein structure was recorded in the Protein Data Bank format and visualised using the PyMOL Molecular Graphics System. Comparing the derived allele frequency of the positively selected variants with that of neutral variants outside genic regions and CpG islands for each dataset was performed to indicate selective signature for local adaptation.

Ethics and inclusion statement
As per the Health Equity Research Outcomes and improvement Consortium (HEROIC) Prostate Cancer Precision Health (PCaPH) Africa 1K inter-institutional Collaborative Research Agreement (CRA), which includes generating regionally representative Panel of Normal (PoN) genomes, including Namibia and South Africa, and the Global Code of Conduct for research in resource-poor settings, locals have been included in all aspects of the research including study design, local primary ethics approvals and stewardship, study implementation, analysis and authorship, to intellectual property and data ownership. Capacity building across the region includes (i) awarded and self-managed budget allocation to South Africa, which has led to numerous employments, (ii) sourcing infrastructure, resourcing and providing clinical training, (iii) co-supervision and exchanges for postgraduate students to genomic intensive partner laboratories, (iv) providing access to off-site high performance computational infrastructure, while (v) holding local training workshops in genomics. Through engagement and inclusion of local policymakers, local conservancy and public health leaders, the team is committed to the dissemination of scientific data back to communities and local government.

In addition, although the authors filtered out samples based on admixture proportion, they still retained samples with up to 22% of admixture (median 0%, range 0-22%). • Line 283 ‘[…] genetic separation observed at 20kya consistent with the observation of basal Eurasian …’: In this paper the authors give a lower bound based on the time of the ancient sample they used (>24 kya). I think the separation is >35kya: Fu, Meyer, Stenzel et al. PNAS.2012; Malaspinas et al. Nature.2016; Choin et al.Nature. 2016 (the two last estimated divergence between Sardinians and Han ~40kya).
A previous study (Pickrell, Patterson, Barbieri et al. Nature Communication.2012) using genotyping array suggests “Damara were a non-Khoisan population who acquired their language from their Khoisan neighbours (the Nama) with little Khoisan gene flow”.
Schlebusch, Skoglund, Sjodin et al. Science. 2012 also found an East African connexion for the Nama population and ‘suggest that they originate from a Southern San group that adopted pastoralism with some introgression from an East African group that potentially brought pastoralist practices.‘

### Reviewer 3

Jaratlerdsiri and colleagues report about 150 new high-coverage Southern African genomes from Namibia. The coverage of several different groups makes this a highly valuable dataset. Unfortunately, the analysis presented in the paper does not do justice to this unique dataset. I have outlined my major concerns about the data and the analyses below.
1. Ethics, consent, and sharing: The manuscript does not provide sufficient details on the data collection. Given that these genomes are from highly marginalized populations that have previously been aggrieved by genomics research, it is pivotal that the ethical aspects of the study are evaluated critically.
i. Firstly, did the Namibian San council approve the study? Proof of approval needs to be provided.
ii. A full section on the recruitment of the participants and the ethics are provided. This should answer questions such as:
a. When were the Kho-San participants recruited? Who performed the recruitment?
b. What did the participant information sheet/Case report form say?
c. How were the concepts of whole genome sequencing, and secondary data sharing explained?
d. Which languages the informed consents were translated into? Could the participants sign? If not, how it was captured?
e. Did the informed consent have a provision for individual-level data sharing?
f. How will the access to the data be regulated? Who will oversee that?
iii. Could the authors clarify how the "extensive and continued engagement" as mentioned in the manuscript was performed?
a. How many times the participants/communities were visited before the study and how many times they have been contacted after the sample collection?
b. What was the mechanism and frequency of community feedback
a. The author list includes only two authors from Namibia and none of them seem to have expertise in genetics or history – so how was it ensured that the participants/communities understood the key messages and nuances?
2. Population structure: The authors had the unique opportunity to investigate the population structure and correlation between genetics and ethnolinguistic identities of individual San populations. Surprisingly the authors did not compare these genomes to any of the public genomics datasets (Schlebusch et al. 2017, Choudhury et al. 2020, Sengupta et al. 2022, Ragsdale et al. 2023, Tallman et al. 2023, Fortes lima et al. 2023) from Southern Africa that could have a provided a framework to interpret the variations and the structure reported in these novel genomes.
Even in terms of presentation - the 3-dimensional PCA plots with only a few populations are difficult to interpret. Phylogenetic trees with only a subset of genomes were not very informative either. The authors should present their genomes in the backdrop of at least some of the previous datasets and if possible, employ some of the more recent approaches such as UMAP and GCAE to visualize the population structure in a more informative way.
3. Population divergence and demographic history: A 13,000-year split between ǂNūkhoen and Bantu speakers is one of the highlights of the results. However, this does not align with the current understanding and models of African population migration and history. Moreover, this claim is based only on a single method and concerns have been raised about the accuracy of PSMC/MSMC-based population divergence estimates. Therefore, the authors need to employ other approaches such as SMC++ and RELATE that can analyze a larger number of sequences per group to support their claim. Also, it would be useful to check whether the same results are obtained if other proxy Bantu-speaker populations are considered.
As a lot of work needs to be done to support this claim, in case the authors find that it might take a substantial time to do this, they can take this section out.
4. The comparison of European ancestry Australians to Khoe-San to identify lifestyle-associated selection is perhaps the weakest section of the manuscript.
There are several layers of differences – including strikingly different demographic histories (out-of-Africa related and probably tens of strong bottleneck events thereafter in one group), genetic drift, non-random/assortative mating, introgression from groups such as Neanderthal and Denisovans, the geographically stratified impact of pathogens, the impact of different climatic conditions that could have caused these populations to harbor different alleles at different frequencies.
The attempt to relate the differences in the populations with such old divergences and extremely different histories to be just due to “forager" and "Western" lifestyle is not meaningful. Had the comparison been performed to related African populations with different lifestyles it might have still made sense.
Although the dN/dS ratio-based selection scan has been in use for a long time it is rarely employed these days for identifying signatures of selection in humans. In case, the authors believe that this is superior to other well-established (allele frequency-based. LD-based, SFS-based) methods then they need to demonstrate it using specific cases and in-depth comparisons with results from other methods. I am not sure if that is within the scope of the current manuscript. Given that the premise they are applying the selection scan to is in itself problematic. I believe this section should be taken out completely.
Minor comments
1. The scheme of nomenclature is not uniform – the abstract starts with Khoe-San and the introduction say this is a Khoe-San genomic resource, but then the rest of the manuscript goes on to describe the populations as “Southern African forgers”.
2. Several statements that are not well-founded and need to be removed or reframed. For example, the paper states that - "Our forager populations also maintained 21 ancient and inactive AluJo mobile elements (thought to integrate into primate genomes ∼65 million years ago41), again supporting their prehistoric lifestyles."
How do the authors know that the other populations did not lose these elements due to strong bottleneck or genetic drift but that the Khoe-San retained these due to prehistoric lifestyle? Did they check whether these elements are fully absent in all other humans, especially African populations? Is there a reason that the prehistoric lifestyle is benefited by this?
In summary, I would recommend the authors demonstrate that the data was collected, and stored with proper ethics, permissions (especially the San council), and community engagement. They also need to show that they have the necessary permissions from communities/authorities for cross-border sharing of individual-level data.
They need to expand their population structure section and bring in other relevant public datasets. I would recommend the authors take out sections on selection. Also, they need to either provide additional data for supporting the PSMC/MSMC-based claims or take out the section too.
